operations.before: A documented teaching collection shows differences within a population, not a ladder of inherently higher forms.
operations.value: One invented local wolf population starts with 10 faster and 10 slower breeding adults, classified by running records, not appearance. Fleet prey dominates during a food shortage. Both groups retain the other abilities needed to live and catch prey. Speed is advantageous only under the specified conditions, not a universal ranking.

operations.before: Some differences recur across generations. This is not modern DNA knowledge or a complete theory of inheritance.
operations.value: For this toy generation, F1–F5 are five pairs of faster adults; S1–S5 are five pairs of slower adults. Each pair has four pups. Stipulate that offspring retain their parents’ speed category because the difference is inherited, not learned through rearing. Only same-category pairs are included. This supplied premise is not inferred from photographs or from resemblance alone; it does not explain the physical mechanism of inheritance.

operations.before: Many offspring are produced; not all leave offspring of their own under limited conditions.
operations.value: Invented recruitment ledger: each of F1–F5 produces 4 faster pups, of whom 3 reach the next breeding cohort: 20 born, 15 recruited. Each of S1–S5 produces 4 slower pups, of whom 1 recruits: 20 born, 5 recruited. Each pup is counted once under its parental pair. In this stipulated case, speed improves obtaining scarce fleet prey and hence recruitment. The other 20 pups do not breed in this cohort; births alone are not reproductive success.

operations.before: An authored population example records changing frequencies across generations, not a single individual transforming by effort.
operations.value: The first breeding cohort has 10 faster + 10 slower adults = 20. Its 40 offspring supply a separate next breeding cohort: 15 faster + 5 slower = 20. No original adults are included in that second count, and no migrants enter it. Compare the two cohorts, not 20 parents plus 20 recruits. This is one invented transition, not a measured time series or a forecast of later generations.

operations.before: A supplied 1858 dossier records independent reasoning toward natural selection and the joint presentation.
operations.value: One argument said that domestic varieties tending to revert showed natural varieties must remain within fixed bounds. Wallace’s 1858 essay challenged that inference: conditions outside domestication differ, and a variety can persist or depart further when it fits those conditions. He developed his reasoning independently; it was presented with Darwin’s work in 1858. This is a substantive contrasting argument, not just a second signature.

operations.before: Repeated processes and a long history make room for cumulative change; Lyell’s influence does not mean he accepted every evolutionary conclusion.
operations.value: The earlier geological record supplied a sequence of processes, not a biological cause. Long time allows successive inherited changes to accumulate if conditions and reproduction keep favoring them; time alone selects nothing. It cannot turn our one-generation count into a record of an entire species’ past. Lyell’s influence did not mean agreement with every evolutionary conclusion.

operations.before: A population argument is adapted to organisms: more offspring may be produced than reproduce successfully. It is not a moral endorsement of human deprivation.
operations.value: The population pamphlet’s growth constraint becomes a biological question: which offspring join the next breeding cohort? Here 40 pups are born but only 20 recruit under the stated food shortage. Excess offspring supplies a constraint, not an explanation of which trait increases. The ledger must also connect the inherited difference to unequal recruitment. This is not a rule for human institutions.

operations.before: In the supplied environment, some inherited differences affect reproductive success; fitness is contextual, not a universal rank.
operations.value: Birth output is equal: 4 pups per pair in both groups. Recruitment differs: each faster pair contributes 3 next-generation breeders, each slower pair 1. Across five pairs each, that is 15 faster recruits versus 5 slower. Each recruit is counted once, not once for each parent. The model supplies a speed-related feeding advantage under fleet-prey scarcity; a small count alone would not establish that cause.

operations.before: Across generations, frequencies can change. Individuals need not transform in order for populations to evolve.
operations.value: Initial faster share: 10/(10+10) = 10/20 = 50%. Next-cohort faster share: 15/(15+5) = 15/20 = 75%. That is a rise of 25 percentage points, while the cohort total stays 20. The slower share falls from 50% to 25%. The population’s composition changes; the parents do not turn into their faster offspring.

operations.before: Small recurring differences can accumulate over long periods. No inevitable destination or global improvement is built into the mechanism.
operations.value: The 50% → 75% shift follows from existing faster/slower variation, stipulated transmission, and the supplied difference in breeding recruitment under fleet-prey scarcity. This one-generation model does not reconstruct the history of all species.

operations.before: Darwin’s and Wallace’s lines of work meet; the record does not reduce Wallace to a footnote or duplicate ingredient.
operations.value: Our supplied 50% → 75% change does not show whether later generations would return to the starting mixture. Wallace’s argument challenges a supposed compulsory return of natural varieties to an original type; Darwin’s imagined predator case asks how existing differences can be favored under changed prey conditions. These are related, independent lines of reasoning, not identical experiments. Our one transition does not establish indefinite divergence.

operations.before: The case distinguishes evidence, mechanism and unresolved inheritance questions; a powerful theory still invites further tests.
operations.value: Reuse the water investigation’s discipline: separate the recorded contrast from the causal claim. The invented cohort count establishes 50% → 75%; selection follows here because inheritance and speed-related recruitment were supplied as premises. A single small real-world count would not by itself distinguish selection from random sampling (drift), migration, or measurement error. A real investigation needs independent inheritance evidence, recruitment tracking, repeated comparisons and tests of alternatives.

operations.value: The checked edition keeps the ledger and its limits together: 10 faster + 10 slower parents; 40 pups; 15 faster + 5 slower next breeders. Population pressure poses the constraint; deep time permits repetition; evidence discipline prevents overclaiming. This invented example neither proves every species’ history nor supplies a moral or policy rule for human society.

value.title: Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859), IV, pp.90–91 and 95–96: imaginary wolf/prey example and accumulation over time
value.note: Primary text. Darwin explicitly labels the wolf/prey illustration imaginary and requires retention of other needed abilities. Our 20-adult/40-pup/20-recruit counts, exact inheritance, pair grouping and non-overlapping cohorts are authored simplifications, not Darwin’s data.

value.title: Wallace, On the Tendency of Varieties to depart indefinitely from the Original Type (1858), pp.53–62, in the joint Darwin–Wallace publication
value.note: Primary text: opening challenge to inferred permanent natural bounds (pp.53–54), domestic/wild contrast and conclusion (pp.60–62); introductory letter records independent work. No numerical wolf data taken from this source; its caricature of Lamarck is not adopted.
